content: SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, has been identified in non-respiratory specimens, including stool, blood, ocular secretions, and semen. However, the role of these sites in viral transmission remains uncertain. Multiple studies have confirmed the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in stool samples, even in cases where viral RNA is no longer detectable in upper respiratory samples. SARS-CoV-2 antigens have been identified in gastrointestinal epithelial cells obtained from biopsy samples. In rare cases, live SARS-CoV-2 has been cultured from stool samples, suggesting the potential for fecal-oral transmission. A recent study utilized computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to analyze fluid flow during toilet flushing. Simulations demonstrated that toilet flushing generates significant turbulence and vortices, which can aerosolize virus-containing droplets. These droplets may be inhaled or settle on surfaces, potentially contributing to viral spread. However, neither the World Health Organization (WHO) nor the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have confirmed fecal-oral transmission of SARS-CoV-2. While fecal-oral transmission has not been definitively established, it has not been clinically demonstrated as a significant factor in the spread of COVID-19, as noted in a joint WHO-China report. Gastrointestinal Risk Factors for COVID-19 Certain conditions may increase the risk of gastrointestinal complications in COVID-19 patients: Chronic liver diseases, such as cirrhosis. Comorbidities, including Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. Severe obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 40 or higher. Liver transplant recipients. Complications: Diarrhea Diarrhea is an uncommon gastrointestinal symptom in COVID-19 patients but may be the initial presenting symptom in some cases. The reported frequency of diarrhea ranges from 1% to 35%, with variability likely due to differing definitions of diarrhea across studies. Diarrhea is more frequently observed in patients with severe COVID-19 compared to those with milder disease. Patients with gastrointestinal symptoms are also more likely to develop severe respiratory disease, including acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), requiring ventilatory support. Pathophysiology of Diarrhea in COVID-19 SARS-CoV-2 enters cells via angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and the serine protease TMPRSS2 receptors. These receptors are abundantly expressed not only in the lungs but also in the enterocytes of the small intestine, as well as in the upper esophagus, liver, and colon. Viral entry disrupts enterocytes, potentially leading to inflammation and altered intestinal permeability. Diarrhea may also result from alterations in the gut microbiota, which could be influenced by antiviral or antibiotic treatments used in COVID-19 management. Clinical Features of Diarrhea Caused by SARS-CoV-2 According to Jin et al., diarrhea is defined as the passage of loose stools more than three times per day. Approximately 1% of patients experienced diarrhea at the onset of illness, with symptoms lasting around four days. The duration of diarrhea typically ranges from two to four days, with three to eight bowel movements per day, as reported in various studies. Treatment of Diarrhea in COVID-19 Supportive management is the cornerstone of treatment. This includes rehydration, fluid replacement, and monitoring of potassium levels. Probiotics may be beneficial, particularly if diarrhea is caused by alterations in the gut microbiome. Probiotics could also help prevent secondary bacterial infections by restoring gut microbiota balance. Oral Mucosal Lesions Associated with COVID-19 Recent reports, such as those by Carreras-Presas et al., have documented oral vesiculobullous lesions in three patients with COVID-19. The high expression of ACE2 receptors on epithelial cells in the oral cavity facilitates viral entry and infection. This is also thought to explain the presence of coronavirus in human saliva. Dysgeusia in COVID-19 Dysgeusia, or altered taste perception, has been reported as a symptom associated with COVID-19. Hepatic Injury in COVID-19 Several studies have reported liver injury in COVID-19 patients. The exact mechanisms of liver injury remain unclear, but proposed mechanisms include direct viral infection of liver cells, leading to elevated hepatic enzymes. Preliminary studies suggest that ACE2 receptor expression is enriched in cholangiocytes (bile duct cells) rather than hepatocytes, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 may directly bind to ACE2-positive cholangiocytes, disrupting liver function. The detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in stool samples supports the possibility of viral exposure in the liver. Natural History of Hepatic Injury in COVID-19 Patients with severe COVID-19 are more likely to exhibit abnormal liver function. For example, Guan et al. reported that 2% of patients with non-severe disease and 39.4% of those with severe disease had liver dysfunction. Other studies with smaller sample sizes have reported similar findings. Summary COVID-19, while primarily a respiratory disease, can have significant gastrointestinal and hepatic manifestations. These include diarrhea, oral mucosal lesions, dysgeusia, and liver injury. The pathophysiology involves viral entry via ACE2 receptors, which are expressed in various gastrointestinal and hepatic tissues. Treatment is largely supportive, with a focus on managing symptoms and preventing complications.
